**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Design a study in writing under exam conditions. Then take an outline apart — somebody else's, and your own.

## Where to read more

[Adams](https://doi.org/10.4135/9788132108498) ch. 16 on writing and presenting.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

**Midterm.** You are given a situation and asked to design a study to evaluate it, in writing. The question. The design, and the assumption carrying it. What data it requires. And what would undermine it. Open note. It tests whether you can apply the design vocabulary to a situation you have not seen, not whether you memorised definitions. It is the same move the room has made every week since meeting 2, which is why it needs no revision beyond turning up all term.

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

Bring your outline — topic sentences with the evidence noted under each, not prose. Workshop it in rotation. Somebody else reads your skeleton and tells you where the argument jumps, and you do the same for theirs; that pairing is where your referee report comes from. Then how to state a limitation without gutting your own project, and what a referee actually looks for. Then you rate your teammates for the second time.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.

## Due

Proposal outline — workshopped in class · Rate your teammates · Exercise 2 — rebuild and critique a figure, end of week
